title: Short Stuff: Chastity Belts
summary: Short Stuff episode on chastity belts. Josh and Chuck (with a joking aside about Jerry the producer) explain the popular legend that medieval husbands locked their wives in iron chastity belts while away at war. They trace the first mention to Conrad Kyeser von Eichstadt's early fifteenth-century military manuscript Bellifortis, which also contains fanciful inventions, suggesting the device may be a joke. A sixteenth-century German satirical image is cited as further evidence of satire. The hosts then explain that surviving chastity belts mostly date to the nineteenth century, when English manufacturers made them for curiosity shows and museums, and that the British Museum displays one with a placard saying there is no real evidence of medieval use. Historian Albrecht Classen's book The Medieval Chastity Belt: A Myth-Making Process is cited, along with USC professor Lisa Bitel's point that the Middle Ages were not as backward as assumed. The episode closes by noting modern latex chastity devices used in BDSM, which the hosts defer to a future episode.

entities.name: The Medieval Chastity Belt: A Myth-Making Process

segments.title: Opening banter and the chastity belt legend
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the short episode with banter about Jerry and the show's format, then say chastity belts were probably not used for the purpose commonly believed. They describe the legend of a husband locking his wife's genitals away in iron underwear while he went off to war, and discuss how myths like this persist because they make later people feel superior.

segments.title: Bellifortis and the earliest mention
segments.summary: The hosts say the first known mention comes from Konrad Kyeser von Eichstadt, an engineer whose early fifteenth-century manuscript Bellifortis catalogued military devices. The manuscript also includes implausible inventions such as an invisibility machine, a fart-powered device, and a cat-shaped chariot, suggesting Kyeser sometimes included jokes. A sixteenth-century German satirical image showing a husband with donkey ears and a chastity belt is cited as further evidence the device was used as satire.

segments.title: Nineteenth-century origins of surviving belts
segments.summary: Chuck explains that the chastity belts seen in museums mostly date from around the nineteenth century, during a Gothic revival and increased industrialization. English manufacturers reportedly made them as a joke for curiosity shows and museums, which paid to display them. Some museums later removed them after learning they were recent creations passed off as medieval.

segments.title: British Museum placard and Albrecht Classen's book
segments.summary: The British Museum still displays one chastity belt with a placard saying there is no real evidence of medieval creation or use, with evidence described as largely anecdotal or from burlesque fiction. The hosts cite historian Albrecht Classen's book The Medieval Chastity Belt: A Myth-Making Process as the source for the debunking.

segments.title: Re-evaluating the Middle Ages
segments.summary: The hosts argue that medieval people were not simply backward. They note that life was hard without modern medicine, electricity, or plumbing, but that the culture was not stupid, had jokes and satire, and included women writers. They cite USC professor Lisa Bitel on the subject.

segments.title: Modern chastity devices and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts note that modern latex chastity devices exist and are used mostly in BDSM, a topic they defer to a future episode. They then close the short episode with the standard sign-off.
